title: Rabbi Shimon bar Karsana
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: Hyman finds him mentioned only in the Jerusalem Talmud. He was Rabbi Acha’s student and always spoke in Rabbi Acha’s name, as in Shabbat, beginning of halakhah 8 of chapter 1; Eruvin 1:7 (chapter 3, end of halakhah 4; the Rif at the end of chapter 1 of Eruvin reads Rabbi Shimon bar Bisna); Yoma 3:8; Beitzah 5:8; and Avodah Zarah, beginning of chapter 1.

We find in Avodah Zarah 1:1, “Rabbi Shimon bar Barsana in the name of Rabbi Acha,” and Hyman proposes bar Karsana. It became more corrupted in Demai, chapter 3, end of halakhah 1, where it reads “Rabbi Shimon bar Sani in the name of Rabbi Acha”; Hyman proposes bar Karsana. Hyman reconstructs the error by supposing that it was written “bar Karsani”; one “bar” dropped out, the word Karsani was split in two, and from the kaf a bet was made.
He is mentioned in Terumot 2:3, Maaserot 1:2, Challah, chapter 4, end of halakhah 3, and Shabbat, beginning of chapter 3.

We find in Shabbat, beginning of chapter 1, folio 2b: “Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Shimon Karsana”; Hyman proposes “Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yose in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Karsana”; Hyman identifies this Elazar as the later Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yose.

notes.text: Shimon is the student who always reports Acha, not the reverse. All chapter/halakhah references are Jerusalem Talmud; the added word chapter repairs the bare3. Hyman’s Bisna/Barsana/Sani/Karsana reconstructions and letter-loss explanation remain claims, not newly verified print history.

The consulted Jerusalem Talmud Demai 3:1 directly has Shimon bar Karsani reporting Acha. Hyman supplies other forms and reconstructs a letter-loss and word-division history; that reconstruction and the exact Rif reading remain attributed, not newly verified printing history.
